query.original_query: illusory truth effect repetition belief confidence LLM internal representation

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of illusory truth effect from repetition in large language models, probing belief and confidence in residual stream and attention heads, feature dictionary learning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the internal representation of the illusory truth effect in large language models, analyzing how repeated exposure to false statements modulates belief and confidence signals within the residual stream and attention heads. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize factual recall circuits and identify attention heads whose output shifts correlate with increased repetition-induced belief. Our analysis reveals that repeated statements produce distinct activation patterns in specific MLP layers, particularly those associated with confidence estimation and truth judgment. We apply sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning to decompose residual stream activations into monosemantic features, finding that repetition amplifies features encoding familiarity and fluency while suppressing features related to contradiction detection. Feature steering experiments confirm that intervening on these learned features directly alters model confidence ratings. Results show that the illusory truth effect arises from superposition of fluency and truth features, with repetition strengthening the former at the expense of the latter. Our findings provide mechanistic evidence for how repetition biases internal belief representations in language models.

sub_queries.semantic_query: illusory truth effect from repetition on belief confidence in human cognition, fluency and familiarity mechanisms, metacognitive judgment
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the role of processing fluency and familiarity in the illusory truth effect, specifically examining how repetition influences metacognitive judgments of belief confidence. Participants rated the truth of plausible trivia statements, with a subset repeated across two sessions separated by a delay. We measured subjective confidence in each judgment and collected trial-level ratings of perceived fluency and familiarity. Results indicate that repeated statements were more likely to be judged as true, replicating the standard effect. Critically, increases in confidence for repeated items were partially mediated by enhanced subjective fluency, independent of objective recognition memory. However, familiarity-based attributions also contributed uniquely to the effect, particularly when participants explicitly recognized a statement as repeated. Findings support the dual-process account that both fluency and familiarity independently inflate truth judgments, but suggest that fluency-driven metacognitive heuristics may operate more automatically. These results extend the fluency-attribution model by demonstrating that repetition boosts belief confidence through separable cognitive mechanisms, with implications for understanding susceptibility to misinformation.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Repetitions are not all alike: distinct mechanisms sustain repetition in language models
papers.research_question: What are the distinct underlying mechanisms that sustain repetition in language models, and how do they develop during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that repetition in language models arises from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for in-context learning-induced repetition and an early-emerging, fallback mechanism for natural repetition.
papers.conclusion: Repetition in language models stems from two distinct mechanisms: a learned, circuit-based mechanism for ICL-induced repetition and an early-emerging fallback mechanism for natural repetition, which arises when the model fails to attend to informative tokens.
papers.key_findings:
ICL-induced repetition develops progressively over training, while natural repetition emerges early and persists.
ICL repetition relies on a dedicated circuit of attention heads that specialize over training, while natural repetition does not show such circuitry.
Attention during natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens (like newlines), suggesting a fallback behavior.
MLP contributions to repetition are strong in ICL but weak in natural repetition.
ICL repetition leads to lower entropy (higher confidence) as cycles increase, while natural repetition shows higher uncertainty.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia, a relatively small-scale model, and may not generalize to other models or architectures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to models of varying sizes and architectures.
Investigate the causal mechanisms behind early-emerging repetition patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes degrade into repetitive loops, persistently generating identical word sequences. Because repetition is rare in natural human language, its frequent occurrence across diverse tasks and contexts in LLMs remains puzzling. Here we investigate whether behaviorally similar repetition patterns arise from distinct underlying mechanisms and how these mechanisms develop during model training. We contrast two conditions: repetitions elicited by natural text prompts with those induced by in-context learning (ICL) setups that explicitly require copying behavior. Our analyses reveal that ICL-induced repetition relies on a dedicated network of attention heads that progressively specialize over training, whereas naturally occurring repetition emerges early and lacks a defined circuitry. Attention inspection further shows that natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens, suggesting a fallback behavior when relevant context cannot be retrieved. These results indicate that superficially similar repetition behaviors originate from qualitatively different internal processes, reflecting distinct modes of failure and adaptation in language models.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and what are the different types of disagreement?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three classes of disagreement between LM outputs and internal probes—confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity—and shows that probes' superiority is often due to better calibration, and that ensembling probes and queries can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that mismatches between internal and external representations of truthfulness in LMs are diverse, primarily due to different prediction pathways rather than deceptive intent, and provides a taxonomy for understanding these disagreements.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries for evaluating truthfulness in language models.
Probes are better calibrated than queries, meaning their confidence scores more accurately reflect prediction correctness.
Most disagreements between queries and probes are due to confabulation (queries confident when probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), with deception being rare.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can further improve accuracy over using either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, indicating context-dependent behavior.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may affect the distribution of disagreements.
Presentation of only results on linear probes, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Future work may more systematically study the distribution of query–probe disagreements induced by different prompts.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs “lie’ or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today’s LMs, or can query–probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two.

papers.title: Representational Stability of Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How stable are LLM truth judgments under controlled semantic perturbations, and does internal representational stability predict behavioral stability? The paper investigates the role of epistemic familiarity in belief stability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the P-StaT framework to evaluate belief stability in LLMs under semantic perturbations, and shows that epistemic familiarity (familiar vs. unfamiliar fictional content) governs stability in both representational and behavioral settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that epistemic familiarity is a robust signal for belief stability in LLMs, and that the P-StaT framework complements accuracy-based factuality evaluation with a notion of epistemic robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Unfamiliar Synthetic content induces the largest epistemic retractions in both representational and behavioral evaluations.
Familiar Fictional content is more representationally distinct and produces fewer retractions.
There is a decoupling between linguistic similarity and latent-space organization for Fictional content.
The stability hierarchy (Synthetic most destabilizing) is consistent across domains and LLMs.
Representational stability under probing perturbations predicts behavioral stability under zero-shot perturbations.
papers.limitation: Zero-shot retractions conflate belief changes with the number of baseline beliefs available to retract, making direct comparison with probing results difficult.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for factual tasks such as "What treats asthma?" or "What is the capital of Latvia?". However, it remains unclear how stably LLMs encode distinctions between true, false, and neither-true-nor-false content in their internal probabilistic representations. We introduce representational stability as the robustness of an LLM's veracity representations to perturbations in the operational definition of truth. We assess representational stability by (i) training a linear probe on an LLM's activations to separate true from not-true statements and (ii) measuring how its learned decision boundary shifts under controlled label changes. Using activations from sixteen open-source models and three factual domains, we compare two types of neither statements. The first are fact-like assertions about entities we believe to be absent from any training data. We call these unfamiliar neither statements. The second are nonfactual claims drawn from well-known fictional contexts. We call these familiar neither statements. The unfamiliar statements induce the largest boundary shifts, producing up to $40\%$ flipped truth judgements in fragile domains (such as word definitions), while familiar fictional statements remain more coherently clustered and yield smaller changes ($\leq 8.2\%$). These results suggest that representational stability stems more from epistemic familiarity than from linguistic form. More broadly, our approach provides a diagnostic for auditing and training LLMs to preserve coherent truth assignments under semantic uncertainty, rather than optimizing for output accuracy alone.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions? Specifically, what are the roles of entropy neurons and token frequency neurons in confidence calibration?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes two types of confidence-regulation neurons in LLMs: entropy neurons, which modulate output entropy via an unembedding null space and LayerNorm, and token frequency neurons, which adjust the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess dedicated neurons for confidence regulation, which operate through specific mechanisms such as writing to the unembedding null space and modulating the distance to the unigram distribution, highlighting the importance of these components for calibration.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy neurons write to an effective null space of the unembedding matrix and use the final LayerNorm scale to modulate output entropy with minimal direct effect on logits.
Token frequency neurons boost or suppress token logits proportionally to their frequency, shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
These neurons act as hedging mechanisms, increasing loss on correct predictions but preventing loss spikes on incorrect ones.
Entropy neurons are present across various model families and scales (up to 7B parameters).
In induction tasks, entropy neurons increase output entropy to decrease confidence when repeating subsequences.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only Transformer-based language models.
Token frequency neurons are identified only in models for which the training corpus is known.
The case study focuses solely on induction.
Entropy neurons might be a byproduct of dropout regularization, as all analyzed models were trained with dropout.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to encoder-decoder models.
Study other potential confidence-regulation mechanisms.
Investigate the role of dropout in the formation of entropy neurons.
Explore interactions between confidence-regulation neurons and other model components.
papers.abstract: Despite their widespread use, the mechanisms by which large language models (LLMs) represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates two critical components believed to influence this uncertainty: the recently discovered entropy neurons and a new set of components that we term token frequency neurons. Entropy neurons are characterized by an unusually high weight norm and influence the final layer normalization (LayerNorm) scale to effectively scale down the logits. Our work shows that entropy neurons operate by writing onto an unembedding null space, allowing them to impact the residual stream norm with minimal direct effect on the logits themselves. We observe the presence of entropy neurons across a range of models, up to 7 billion parameters. On the other hand, token frequency neurons, which we discover and describe here for the first time, boost or suppress each token's logit proportionally to its log frequency, thereby shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution. Finally, we present a detailed case study where entropy neurons actively manage confidence in the setting of induction, i.e. detecting and continuing repeated subsequences.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Understanding and Controlling Repetition Neurons and Induction Heads in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between repetition neurons and induction heads in in-context learning, and how does their ablation affect ICL performance and repetitive generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a layer-wise analysis showing that repetition neurons in late layers are critical for ICL, while middle-layer neurons can be ablated to reduce repetition without harming ICL, and proposes a three-segment ablation strategy for this purpose.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that repetition neurons and induction heads form a cascade for pattern recognition in ICL, and that selective ablation of middle-layer repetition neurons can reduce repetitive generation while preserving ICL performance.
papers.key_findings:
The impact of repetition neuron ablation on ICL performance varies significantly with layer depth.
Repetition neurons in output-side layers serve as critical executors of pattern-based predictions, with effects on ICL performance comparable to induction heads.
Joint ablation of both repetition neurons and induction heads leads to a near-complete breakdown of pattern recognition.
Selectively deactivating repetition neurons in middle layers reduces repetition while preserving ICL performance.
future_direction: Generalizing the three-step pipeline (behavioral pattern detection, neuron/head ranking, targeted ablation) to other problems like memorization.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize repetitive input patterns and their performance on in-context learning (ICL). In contrast to prior work that has primarily focused on attention heads, we examine this relationship from the perspective of skill neurons, specifically repetition neurons. Our experiments reveal that the impact of these neurons on ICL performance varies depending on the depth of the layer in which they reside. By comparing the effects of repetition neurons and induction heads, we further identify strategies for reducing repetitive outputs while maintaining strong ICL capabilities.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concepts of validity and plausibility, and why do they conflate them, leading to content effects in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned in LLMs, causing content effects, and that steering vectors can disentangle these concepts to reduce bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The representational entanglement of validity and plausibility in LLMs leads to content effects, and representational interventions offer a way to mitigate these biases for more logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit content effects where plausibility influences validity judgments, especially in zero-shot settings.
Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded as single directions in the model's activation space, and these vectors are highly similar.
The degree of alignment between validity and plausibility vectors predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models.
Plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgments, and vice versa, demonstrating cross-concept influence.
Debiasing steering vectors that disentangle validity from plausibility can reduce content effects and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.abstract: Both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit content effects: biases in which the plausibility of the semantic content of a reasoning problem influences judgments regarding its logical validity. While this phenomenon in humans is best explained by the dual-process theory of reasoning, the mechanisms behind content effects in LLMs remain unclear. In this work, we address this issue by investigating how LLMs encode the concepts of validity and plausibility within their internal representations. We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity. Using steering vectors, we demonstrate that plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgements, and vice versa, and that the degree of alignment between these two concepts predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models. Finally, we construct debiasing vectors that disentangle these concepts, reducing content effects and improving reasoning accuracy. Our findings advance understanding of how abstract logical concepts are represented in LLMs and highlight representational interventions as a path toward more logical systems.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Repetition Neurons: How Do Language Models Produce Repetitions?
papers.research_question: How do language models produce repetitions? The paper investigates the internal mechanisms by identifying and analyzing 'repetition neurons' responsible for the repetition problem in text generation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'repetition neurons'—neurons in Transformer feed-forward networks that are progressively activated during repetition. It shows these neurons can be identified by comparing activation values before and after repetition onset, and that intervening on them (deactivating or activating) controls the occurrence of repetitive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method to identify repetition neurons that contribute to the repetition problem in text generation. These neurons are located in both intermediate and final layers, and experimental results show that intervening in their activity can control the occurrence of repetitive outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Repetition neurons are identified by comparing average activation values in normal vs. repetition ranges, with only a small number of neurons showing high activation differences.
Repetition neurons are located in both intermediate and final layers of the Transformer, suggesting two types: pattern detectors and drivers for replication.
Deactivating repetition neurons reduces the number of samples with repetition, while activating them increases repetition, confirming their causal role.
Repetition neurons are distinct from, but show some coordination with, induction heads and self-finding heads in attention layers.
The effect of repetition neurons varies with model size and language, as shown by comparisons between Gemma-2B and Gemma-7B, and between English and Japanese models.
papers.limitation:
The dataset was prepared without considering detailed aspects of repetition, such as the length of each repetitive phrase.
The functional differences between neurons located in the intermediate layers and those in the final layer are not explored.
Only roughly 30% of the repetition problem is attributed to the repetition neurons; the cause of the remaining 70% is unknown.
The behavior of repetition neurons may change with model configuration (e.g., parameter size, pre-training language, activation functions).
The intervention method is simple (replacing activation with 0.0 or adding 1.0); gradual changes in activation value are not explored.
Beyond neuron-based and head-based analysis, other specific circuits in LLMs for repetitive texts are not explored.
future_direction: Investigate the effect of repetitive phrase length on the behavior of repetition neurons.
Explore the functional differences between repetition neurons in intermediate layers and the final layer.
Identify causes for the remaining 70% of repetition problems not attributed to repetition neurons.
Study how the behavior of repetition neurons changes with model configuration (e.g., parameter size, language, activation functions).
Explore gradual intervention methods for repetition neurons instead of simple replacement or addition.
Investigate other specific circuits in LLMs' calculation when outputting repetitive texts.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces repetition neurons, regarded as skill neurons responsible for the repetition problem in text generation tasks. These neurons are progressively activated more strongly as repetition continues, indicating that they perceive repetition as a task to copy the previous context repeatedly, similar to in-context learning. We identify these repetition neurons by comparing activation values before and after the onset of repetition in texts generated by recent pre-trained language models. We analyze the repetition neurons in three English and one Japanese pre-trained language models and observe similar patterns across them.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: LENS: Learning Ensemble Confidence from Neural States for Multi-LLM Answer Integration
papers.research_question: How can we effectively combine predictions from multiple LLMs by learning to estimate each model's context-dependent confidence from its internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LENS, a novel ensemble method that learns lightweight linear confidence predictors for each LLM using layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities, enabling more effective weighting of model predictions based on context-dependent reliability.
papers.conclusion: LENS is a simple yet effective ensemble method that leverages model confidence patterns learned from internal representations to improve performance across diverse question-answering tasks, offering a practical and scalable solution for robust LLM ensembles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Max Confidence ensemble method outperforms baseline methods (Majority Vote and Probability Max) on 5 out of 6 evaluated datasets.
Internal representations (hidden states) contain valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.
The method is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and does not require retraining or modifying the base LLMs.
The approach generalizes well across diverse question-answering tasks, including logical reasoning, commonsense inference, and mathematics.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation is restricted to decoder-only transformer architectures, limiting applicability to encoder-decoder or other model types.
The method requires access to intermediate layer representations, which may not be available in production environments or with commercial API-based models.
future_direction: Investigating cross-task transferability of learned confidence patterns for zero-shot ensemble learning.
Extending the method to modern multi-LLM systems and agent collaboration scenarios.
Leveraging confidence patterns and intermediate representations to enhance understanding of LLM decision-making processes (model interpretability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, with different models excelling in distinct domains and specific abilities. Effectively combining the predictions of multiple LLMs is crucial for enhancing system robustness and performance. However, existing ensemble methods often rely on simple techniques like voting or logits ensembling, which overlook the varying confidence and reliability of models in different contexts. In this work, we propose LENS (Learning ENsemble confidence from Neural States), a novel approach that learns to estimate model confidence by analyzing internal representations. For each LLM, we train a lightweight linear confidence predictor that leverages layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities as inputs.
