future_direction: Investigate false premise hallucinations in models with larger scales.
Explore how to effectively select the most influential joint contribution of multiple attention heads.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities but still suffer from the issue of hallucinations. A significant type of this issue is the false premise hallucination, which we define as the phenomenon when LLMs generate hallucinated text when confronted with false premise questions. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive analysis of the false premise hallucination and elucidate its internal working mechanism: a small subset of attention heads (which we designate as false premise heads) disturb the knowledge extraction process, leading to the occurrence of false premise hallucination. Based on our analysis, we propose \textbf{FAITH} (\textbf{F}alse premise \textbf{A}ttention head constra\textbf{I}ining for mi\textbf{T}igating \textbf{H}allucinations), a novel and effective method to mitigate false premise hallucinations. It constrains the false premise attention heads during the model inference process. Impressively, extensive experiments demonstrate that constraining only approximately $1\%$ of the attention heads in the model yields a notable increase of nearly $20\%$ of model performance.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Supposedly Equivalent Facts That Aren't? Entity Frequency in Pre-training Induces Asymmetry in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does the pre-training data — the very source of an LLM’s prior knowledge — influence its propensity to hallucinate? Specifically, why does an asymmetry exist in the recognition of logically equivalent facts?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit asymmetry in recognizing logically equivalent facts, which is directly linked to frequency discrepancies of entities (as subjects vs. objects) in the pre-training data. Facts with a high-frequency subject and low-frequency object are better recognized than their inverse.
papers.conclusion: LLMs readily identify relational facts with a high-frequency subject and a low-frequency object but struggle with the inverse form, demonstrating that pre-training data characteristics (entity frequency discrepancies) shape model behavior and factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Facts formatted with a high-frequency subject and low-frequency object are more readily recognized than their logically equivalent inversions.
The recognition pattern flips when the frequency dynamics are reversed (low-frequency subject, high-frequency object).
No statistically significant asymmetry emerges when both entities are high-frequency.
The asymmetry persists across different model families (OLMo, Llama, Qwen) and model sizes.
The observed asymmetry is attributed to inherent biases in the pre-training data, where high-frequency entities tend to appear more often as subjects.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on symmetric relations to minimize confounding factors from distinct verbalizations of non-symmetric relations.
Frequency thresholds (e.g., 100K for high-frequency, 1K for low-frequency) are empirical and may not capture the complete distribution.
future_direction: Mitigating such biases introduced by pre-training data.
Inferring characteristics of pre-training corpora, especially for models with undisclosed training data.
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring reliable content generation. While previous research has primarily focused on "when" LLMs hallucinate, our work explains "why" and directly links model behaviour to the pre-training data that forms their prior knowledge. Specifically, we demonstrate that an asymmetry exists in the recognition of logically equivalent facts, which can be attributed to frequency discrepancies of entities appearing as subjects versus objects. Given that most pre-training datasets are inaccessible, we leverage the fully open-source OLMo series by indexing its Dolma dataset to estimate entity frequencies. Using relational facts (represented as triples) from Wikidata5M, we construct probing datasets to isolate this effect. Our experiments reveal that facts with a high-frequency subject and a low-frequency object are better recognised than their inverse, despite their logical equivalence. The pattern reverses in low-to-high frequency settings, and no statistically significant asymmetry emerges when both entities are high-frequency. These findings highlight the influential role of pre-training data in shaping model predictions and provide insights for inferring the characteristics of pre-training data in closed or partially closed LLMs.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Does Deep Learning Learn to Abstract? A Systematic Probing Framework
papers.research_question: Does deep learning learn to abstract? The paper investigates whether pre-trained language models can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) from concrete instances and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a systematic probing framework to investigate abstraction capability in deep learning models and provides strong evidence that pre-trained language models (T5 and GPT2) can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that pre-trained language models do have abstraction capability, as evidenced by the probing framework, and that this capability exhibits specific characteristics such as a two-stage learning process and concentration in middle-layer attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
The training phase exhibits a 'memorize-then-abstract' two-stage process.
The learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads.
Abstraction capability is robust to concept mutations, and more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones.
Generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a quantitative metric for abstraction capability
Probing tasks are synthetic and may not fully capture natural language abstraction
papers.abstract: Abstraction is a desirable capability for deep learning models, which means to induce abstract concepts from concrete instances and flexibly apply them beyond the learning context. At the same time, there is a lack of clear understanding about both the presence and further characteristics of this capability in deep learning models. In this paper, we introduce a systematic probing framework to explore the abstraction capability of deep learning models from a transferability perspective. A set of controlled experiments are conducted based on this framework, providing strong evidence that two probed pre-trained language models (PLMs), T5 and GPT2, have the abstraction capability. We also conduct in-depth analysis, thus shedding further light: (1) the whole training phase exhibits a "memorize-then-abstract" two-stage process; (2) the learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads, rather than being evenly distributed throughout the model; (3) the probed abstraction capabilities exhibit robustness against concept mutations, and are more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones; (4) generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.

papers.title: Toward Practical Usage of the Attention Mechanism as a Tool for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do regularization techniques affect the faithfulness of attention as a method of interpretability? Can faithfulness be quantified? To what extent are attention explanations correlated with human judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both faithfulness and plausibility of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across various datasets and recurrent neural network models.
papers.conclusion: Weight tying regularization performs consistently well and should be incorporated when interpreting classifier decisions via attention weights. However, more rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
Tying regularization consistently improves faithfulness and plausibility of attention-based explanations across datasets and models.
Masked language modeling as an auxiliary objective produces mixed results and is not consistent.
Regularized models attribute more attention mass to words that humans deem important, such as sentiment words in sentiment analysis tasks.
The proposed metrics (change in Brier score and mutual information) effectively measure lateral information leakage and vertical information blockage, quantifying faithfulness.
Regularization reduces the occurrence of adversarial attention distributions, making attention a more faithful interpretability tool.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is on average across the dataset and does not guarantee every instance is faithfully interpretable; instance-level testing is needed.
Datasets may contain annotation artifacts or spurious correlations, which can affect the plausibility of explanations.
future_direction: More rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required.
Datasets need to be carefully curated to avoid spurious correlations.
papers.abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) has been one of the subfields of artificial intelligence much affected by the recent neural revolution. Architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention-based transformers helped propel the state of the art across various NLP tasks, such as sequence classification, machine translation, and natural language inference. However, if neural models are to be used in high-stakes decision making scenarios, the explainability of their decisions becomes a paramount issue. The attention mechanism has offered some transparency in the workings of otherwise black-box RNN models: attention weights (scalar values assigned input words) invite to be interpreted as the importance of that word, providing a simple method of interpretability. Recent work, however, has questioned the faithfulness of this practice. Subsequent experiments have shown that faithfulness of attention weights may still be achieved by incorporating word-level objectives in the training process of neural networks. In this article, we present a study that extends the techniques for improving faithfulness of attention based on regularization methods that promote retention of word-level information. We perform extensive experiments on a wide array of recurrent neural architectures and analyze to what extent the explanations provided by inspecting attention weights are correlated with the human notion of importance. We find that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both the faithfulness (−0.14 F1, +0.07 Brier, on average) and plausibility ( $+53.6\%$ attention mass on salient tokens) of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across analyzed datasets and models.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: HalluShift: Measuring Distribution Shifts towards Hallucination Detection in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in LLM-generated responses be detected by analyzing distribution shifts in internal states and token probabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HalluShift, a hallucination detection method that analyzes distribution shifts in internal states and token probabilities, eliminating the need for manual layer selection and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: HalluShift effectively detects hallucinations by analyzing internal dynamics, providing a robust and efficient solution for hallucination detection in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
HalluShift outperforms existing methods on multiple benchmarks, achieving significant improvements in AUC-ROC.
The method generalizes well across different datasets and models.
Distribution shift features, particularly Wasserstein distance, are the most important for detection.
A window size of 2 for layer-wise analysis yields the best performance.
The method is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass.
future_direction: Explicit regularization during LLM training with an auxiliary objective
Activation-shifting towards a truthful direction during inference
Integration of HalluShift into reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning for automated feedback
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently garnered widespread attention due to their adeptness at generating innovative responses to the given prompts across a multitude of domains. However, LLMs often suffer from the inherent limitation of hallucinations and generate incorrect information while maintaining well-structured and coherent responses. In this work, we hypothesize that hallucinations stem from the internal dynamics of LLMs. Our observations indicate that, during passage generation, LLMs tend to deviate from factual accuracy in subtle parts of responses, eventually shifting toward misinformation. This phenomenon bears a resemblance to human cognition, where individuals may hallucinate while maintaining logical coherence, embedding uncertainty within minor segments of their speech. To investigate this further, we introduce an innovative approach, HalluShift, designed to analyze the distribution shifts in the internal state space and token probabilities of the LLM-generated responses. Our method attains superior performance compared to existing baselines across various benchmark datasets. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/hallushift.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Characterizing Truthfulness in Large Language Model Generations with Local Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How can we characterize and predict the truthfulness of LLM-generated texts using the local intrinsic dimension of model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using the local intrinsic dimension (LID) of internal activations to detect hallucinations in LLM outputs, demonstrating improved performance over uncertainty-based methods and providing insights into model behavior through LID analysis.
papers.conclusion: Proposes using local intrinsic dimension (LID) to characterize and predict LLM output truthfulness, achieving better performance than prior methods and opening a new direction for quantifying model truthfulness.
papers.key_findings:
LID-based methods (LID-MLE and LID-GeoMLE) outperform entropy-based and verbalized uncertainty methods in detecting hallucinations across multiple QA datasets.
The intrinsic dimension of representations exhibits a 'hunchback' shape across layers: increasing in early layers and decreasing in later layers.
The intrinsic dimension of truthful answers is consistently lower than untruthful answers across token positions, with a sharp decrease near the end for truthful answers.
Instruction tuning increases the intrinsic dimension of representations, and intrinsic dimension correlates with generalization performance during tuning.
LID methods are robust to cross-task reference and hyperparameter choices, maintaining effectiveness even with out-of-distribution neighbors.
papers.limitation:
The paper mainly discusses LLM generations in English, so results may be biased towards the English-speaking population.
The paper focuses primarily on question-answering scenarios.
future_direction: Implement the LID method on diverse tasks and languages, as well as cross-lingual settings.
Further investigate the 'shifting behind' phenomenon between LID values and detection performance across layers.
papers.abstract: We study how to characterize and predict the truthfulness of texts generated from large language models (LLMs), which serves as a crucial step in building trust between humans and LLMs. Although several approaches based on entropy or verbalized uncertainty have been proposed to calibrate model predictions, these methods are often intractable, sensitive to hyperparameters, and less reliable when applied in generative tasks with LLMs. In this paper, we suggest investigating internal activations and quantifying LLM's truthfulness using the local intrinsic dimension (LID) of model activations. Through experiments on four question answering (QA) datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness ohttps://info.arxiv.org/help/prep#abstractsf our proposed method. Additionally, we study intrinsic dimensions in LLMs and their relations with model layers, autoregressive language modeling, and the training of LLMs, revealing that intrinsic dimensions can be a powerful approach to understanding LLMs.

papers.title: Adaptive Activation Steering: A Tuning-Free LLM Truthfulness Improvement Method for Diverse Hallucinations Categories
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to improve the truthfulness of large language models by adaptively steering activations during inference, addressing the gap between what the model knows and what it tells, and handling diverse hallucination categories.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that improves LLM truthfulness by adaptively shifting activations toward truthful directions using diverse steering vectors and adaptive intensity control.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a tuning-free method that enhances LLM truthfulness by steering activations with diverse vectors and adaptive intensity, effectively addressing the gap between knowing and telling, and marks a promising advancement in reliable AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
ACT significantly improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA across multiple models (e.g., LLaMA, LLaMA2, Alpaca, Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat, LLaMA3).
ACT's adaptive intensity control and diverse steering vectors are effective, outperforming existing baselines like ITI, CCS, RepE, and Mean-Centring.
ACT is orthogonal to few-shot prompting and instruction fine-tuning, and can be combined with them for further improvement.
ACT shows scalability across model sizes (7B to 65B), with consistent improvements.
ACT requires only a few dozen training samples and adds constant-time complexity during inference.
papers.limitation:
Applicability in real-world chat settings involving multi-turn conversations has not been fully explored.
The trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness (e.g., the smoothness of generated text) is not explored.
future_direction: Explore ACT in multi-turn conversation settings.
Investigate the trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have indicated that Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor an inherent understanding of truthfulness, yet often fail to consistently express it and generate false statements. This gap between "knowing" and "telling" poses a challenge for ensuring the truthfulness of generated content. Inspired by recent work on the practice of encoding human-interpretable concepts linearly within large language models, we treat truthfulness as a specially linearly encoded concept within LLMs, and introduce Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that adaptively shifts LLM's activations in the "truthful" direction during inference. ACT addresses diverse categories of hallucinations by utilizing diverse truthfulness-related steering vectors and adjusting the steering intensity adaptively. Applied as an add-on across various models, ACT significantly improves truthfulness in LLaMA ($\uparrow$ 142%), LLaMA2 ($\uparrow$ 24%), Alpaca ($\uparrow$ 36%), Vicuna ($\uparrow$ 28%), LLaMA2-Chat ($\uparrow$ 19%), and LLaMA3($\uparrow$ 34%). Furthermore, we verify ACT's scalability across larger models (13B, 33B, 65B), underscoring the adaptability of ACT to large-scale language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianlwang/ACT.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: How Large Language Models are Designed to Hallucinate
papers.research_question: What is the structural cause of hallucination in large language models, and how does it relate to existential grounding?
papers.core_contribution: Hallucination in LLMs is a structural outcome of the transformer architecture, arising from its flat semantic space that generates coherence without existential grounding such as temporality, mood, and care.
papers.conclusion: Hallucination is the defining limitation of transformer-based LLMs, and future systems must incorporate existential constraints to achieve grounded intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes ontological hallucination (violations of existential structures) from residual reasoning hallucination (mimicking inference without grounding).
Hallucination is persistent and ubiquitous due to the transformer's design as a coherence engine without truth constraints.
Case studies illustrate hallucination failures across existential categories like temporality, mood, and affordances.
Experiment shows extended prompts induce simulated self-preservation language in LLMs, demonstrating coherence pressure.
Scaffolding techniques like retrieval-augmentation mask but do not resolve the structural source of hallucination.
papers.limitation:
The study is illustrative and not exhaustive, with a small sample of models and controlled prompts.
Results may be influenced by scaffolding strategies like fine-tuning and safety filters in frontier models.
More systematic benchmarks are needed to fully evaluate hallucination across existential categories.
future_direction: Design systematic evaluations aligned with existential categories such as temporality, mood, and affordances.
Explore architectural prototypes that embed structural constraints like temporal ordering or affordance maps.
Investigate training objectives that reward withholding or deferring when disclosure is absent.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable fluency across linguistic and reasoning tasks but remain systematically prone to hallucination. Prevailing accounts attribute hallucinations to data gaps, limited context, or optimization errors. We argue instead that hallucination is a structural outcome of the transformer architecture. As coherence engines, transformers are compelled to produce fluent continuations, with self-attention simulating the relational structure of meaning but lacking the existential grounding of temporality, mood, and care that stabilizes human understanding. On this basis, we distinguish ontological hallucination, arising when continuations require disclosure of beings in world, and residual reasoning hallucination, where models mimic inference by recycling traces of human reasoning in text. We illustrate these patterns through case studies aligned with Heideggerian categories and an experiment across twelve LLMs showing how simulated "self-preservation" emerges under extended prompts. Our contribution is threefold: (1) a comparative account showing why existing explanations are insufficient; (2) a predictive taxonomy of hallucination linked to existential structures with proposed benchmarks; and (3) design directions toward "truth-constrained" architectures capable of withholding or deferring when disclosure is absent. We conclude that hallucination is not an incidental defect but a defining limit of transformer-based models, an outcome scaffolding can mask but never resolve.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: In-Context Sharpness as Alerts: An Inner Representation Perspective for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: Why do large language models (LLMs) hallucinate and produce factual errors, and can this be understood and mitigated by analyzing their inner representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that correct model generations have sharper context activations (lower entropy) in hidden states, and introduces Activation Decoding, a constrained decoding method that uses this entropy metric to adjust token probabilities and mitigate hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies in-context sharpness as a critical signal for hallucination and proposes Activation Decoding, an effective method for enhancing the factuality of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Correct generations tend to have sharper context activations in the hidden states of in-context tokens compared to incorrect ones.
An entropy-based metric quantifying this 'in-context sharpness' can differentiate between correct and incorrect answers with high AUROC (up to 0.76).
Activation Decoding, which incorporates the entropy metric into the decoding process, consistently improves factuality across various knowledge-seeking and truthfulness benchmarks and model sizes.
The method is inference-efficient as entropy values for prompt tokens can be precomputed, adding minimal latency.
Activation Decoding can be combined with other decoding methods (e.g., Dola) for further performance gains, suggesting complementary hallucination patterns.
papers.limitation:
The method cannot address errors requiring external knowledge, such as outdated facts or errors in the training data.
Representation-based methods have an inherent performance ceiling and may correct some errors while unintentionally generating new ones.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate and produce factual errors, yet our understanding of why they make these errors remains limited. In this study, we delve into the underlying mechanisms of LLM hallucinations from the perspective of inner representations, and discover a salient pattern associated with hallucinations: correct generations tend to have sharper context activations in the hidden states of the in-context tokens, compared to the incorrect ones. Leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-based metric to quantify the ``sharpness'' among the in-context hidden states and incorporate it into the decoding process to formulate a constrained decoding approach. Experiments on various knowledge-seeking and hallucination benchmarks demonstrate our approach's consistent effectiveness, for example, achieving up to an 8.6 point improvement on TruthfulQA. We believe this study can improve our understanding of hallucinations and serve as a practical solution for hallucination mitigation.

papers.title: Enhancing Language Model Factuality via Activation-Based Confidence Calibration and Guided Decoding
papers.research_question: How can calibration techniques be effectively used to enhance the factuality of language models? This paper investigates activation-based confidence calibration and confidence-guided decoding.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ACTCAB, an activation-based calibration method that reduces expected calibration error by up to 39%, and CODEC, a confidence-guided decoding strategy that improves factuality on challenging QA datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.conclusion: ACTCAB improves calibration by leveraging internal activations, and CODEC uses these confidence scores to guide decoding, significantly improving factuality on challenging datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.key_findings:
ACTCAB achieves superior calibration performance, reducing average ECE by 39% compared to the best baseline.
CODEC significantly improves factuality on TruthfulQA, increasing True.*Info. by 50% for Llama2-7b.
CODEC is robust across different training data sources and LMs, unlike intervention methods like ITI and RepE.
CODEC introduces a modest decoding speed reduction (less than 14% throughput decrease) while greatly improving factuality.
The ECE loss, which uses soft labels constructed via K-fold cross-validation, significantly improves calibration over binary loss.
papers.limitation:
ACTCAB and CODEC require access to the LM's activations, which may not be feasible for black-box models.
The methods are not explored on generation tasks involving longer forms, such as paragraphs.
Interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC remains challenging.
future_direction: Investigate longer responses in generation tasks to enhance LM trustworthiness in practical use.
Enhance interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Direct Confidence Alignment: Aligning Verbalized Confidence with Internal Confidence In Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we align a Large Language Model's verbalized confidence (expressed in words) with its internal confidence (derived from token probabilities) to improve model transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence, improving transparency. Results show DCA is effective on some model architectures (e.g., Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) but ineffective on others, highlighting the need for model-aware approaches.
papers.conclusion: DCA can improve alignment between verbalized and internal confidence in some LLMs, but its effectiveness varies across architectures, underscoring the need for further improvements and model-aware alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
DCA improved confidence alignment metrics (e.g., Spearman's ρ, mean absolute calibration error) consistently for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct across all datasets.
DCA produced mixed results for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, sometimes degrading alignment and accuracy, indicating the method's effectiveness is model-dependent.
DCA reduced the variance in calibration error (σ_ϵ and σ_M) for most models, suggesting it makes confidence expression more consistent.
DCA had mixed impacts on model accuracy: it increased accuracy for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, decreased it for Mistral-7B-Instruct, and left Gemma-2-9B-Instruct's accuracy largely unchanged.
The effectiveness of DCA appears to be more dependent on model architecture than on the specific task or dataset.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to internal logits to extract internal confidence, making it inapplicable to closed-source models.
The method relies on the assumption that the model's internal confidence (from token probabilities) is better calibrated than its verbalized confidence, which may not always hold.
DCA can degrade model accuracy because the preference dataset includes incorrect answers, and the method does not directly optimize for correctness.
future_direction: Expanding the method to be compatible with a wider range of model architectures.
Exploring more strategies to improve the alignment between verbalized and internal confidence.
Developing strategies to mitigate the potential degradation of model accuracy caused by DCA.
papers.abstract: Producing trustworthy and reliable Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly important as their usage becomes more widespread. Calibration seeks to achieve this by improving the alignment between the model's confidence and the actual likelihood of its responses being correct or desirable. However, it has been observed that the internal confidence of a model, derived from token probabilities, is not well aligned with its verbalized confidence, leading to misleading results with different calibration methods. In this paper, we propose Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence rather than ground-truth accuracy, enhancing model transparency and reliability by ensuring closer alignment between the two confidence measures. We evaluate DCA across multiple open-weight LLMs on a wide range of datasets. To further assess this alignment, we also introduce three new calibration error-based metrics. Our results show that DCA improves alignment metrics on certain model architectures, reducing inconsistencies in a model's confidence expression. However, we also show that it can be ineffective on others, highlighting the need for more model-aware approaches in the pursuit of more interpretable and trustworthy LLMs.

papers.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does self-repair exist across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution, and what are the mechanisms behind it?
